1015.tone: Four level tones plus eleven contour ('deslices') tones, lexically and grammatically contrastive (e.g. rising cluster on the final syllable marks negative verbs and 1pl inclusive). tn.translation: Chiquihuitlán Mazatec is a tonal language. In it there are four tone levels and eleven glides. In writing it, generally no mark is made to indicate the tones. ... The strongest syllable coincides with the highest tone in the word. When the syllables of a word are equally high, the first is the one with the greatest force. ... When the tones rise from one level to another within the same syllable, the syllable is said to carry a rising tonal group. The vowel of that syllable is lengthened a little by the tone and is written with a double vowel.

What it adds to the entry: (1) p. 246 lists 'смыслоразличительное ударение' as a distinguishing feature of Chirag, Kaitag and the southern group; (2) §1 (p. 252, under 'Ударение во многих идиомах является смыслоразличительным', p. 249) files the Chirag pairs under distinctive stress and glosses the second member of each as мальчик\PL[ABS], скирда\PL[ABS]: Kibrik & Kodzasov's own glosses already give the pairs as singular ~ plural ('мальчик' – 'мальчики'), so what is new is the morphological reading of the stress shift as the sole exponent of the plural absolutive; (3) §2.1 (p. 253): 'В десяти исследованных идиомах ударение переходит на показатель множественного числа' with Chirag as the tenth of the ten idioms listed (exx. 53–54, p. 254); the author then cautions (pp. 254–255) that a shift onto the final syllable in absolutive plurals does not by itself prove morphological conditioning — only non-absolutive plural forms would ('полным доказательством морфологической обусловленности перехода, являются любые не абсолютивные формы множественного числа (см. примеры 41–43γ и 50γ)'), and no such Chirag form is given; (4) Table 3 (p. 266), row чираг.: фиксир. '–', см.-разл. '+', ṔL '+', the \PART, MSD, \OBL and syllable-shape columns '?'. evidence_works.detail: Secondhand survey: the memoir states it takes over Veerman-Leichsenring 2000 'point par point' and summarizes Mock 1977. Its §5 'Accent tonique' (p. 26) agrees with the entry's penultimate default ('Dans les mots de deux syllabes ou plus, l'accent tonique tombe en règle générale sur la penultième') and adds: (a) the phonetic cue of stress is vowel length on the stressed syllable or, with a short vowel, gemination of the following consonant ('si2ne2 "jaune" se prononce [si1nne2]'); (b) stress interacts with tone: high tone 'coïncide très souvent avec l'accent tonique; lorsque celui-ci se déplace, le ton baisse' (p. 24, example ta1že1 'son beau-père' vs ta2ža1na1 'mon beau-père'); (c) stress re-locates to keep the penultimate under possessive suffixation ('L'accent tonique tombant en règle générale sur la pénultième, celui-ci se déplace suite à l'ajout du possessif'); (d) enclitics are never stressed ('S'agissant d'enclitiques, l'accent tonique ne tombe jamais sur eux'). None of this changes the coding: (a) matches Mock 1977's own lengthening rules (vowels lengthen in a word-final tonic syllable, p. 28; stops (including nasals) and voiceless fricatives lengthen after a tonic syllable containing a simple vowel), (c) confirms the penultimate rule, (d) is consistent with domain WORD (clitics outside the stress domain), and (b) refines the tone/stress relation within the existing 'tone-and-stress' class. Being a restatement of Veerman-Leichsenring 2000 rather than first-hand data, it cannot recode any field.

1023.dloc: Dunn 1999 sect. 3.6 'Intonation', pp. 53-54 (archive.org scan 2-up pp. 40-41); also sect. 3.4 'Prosodic Phonemes', p. 47: 'Chukchi does not have phonemic stress.' || Kenstowicz 1994 ROA-33 sect. 4 pp. 10-11 (base-final rule, exx. 18-19) and p. 13 (Skorik p. 70 schwa clause).
1023.heavy: Dunn: a syllable 'with a consonant onset and a full vowel' (full = non-schwa). Skorik via Kenstowicz: sonority grades a, e, o > i, u > schwa; a schwa nucleus in the base-final syllable sends stress to a preceding full vowel.
1023.dflt: Dunn: not stated (no all-schwa / all-onsetless word discussed). Skorik via Kenstowicz (p. 70): if both the base-final and the preceding syllable are schwa, stress stays on the base-final syllable.
1023.prule: Two primary descriptions place primary stress differently and are not reconciled by either. (a) Dunn 1999 (Telqep spoken Chukchi, 1990s fieldwork): stress non-phonemic and hard to hear; primary stress on the LEFTMOST syllable of the word that has a consonant onset and a full (non-schwa) vowel, skipping schwa syllables and a vowel-initial first syllable (nú.tec.qə̀.rə.kù.kin, qə.jét.ɣʔi, kə̀r.ɣə.ré.cʔə.kìn, a.tók.tor.kà); alternating secondary stress in both directions. (b) Skorik 1961:67-71 (literary/standard Chukchi; reached only as reported with data in Kenstowicz 1994): stress bound to the base, never on an inflectional suffix; on the base-FINAL syllable when a syllabic suffix follows (pójg-a, winrét-ək, jará-ŋa, weló-lgən, reqoká-lgən, migcirét-ək), retracted off the base-final syllable when it is word-final or the suffix is vowelless (jéjwel; qorá-ŋa but qóra-t), retracted from a base-final high vowel to a more sonorous preceding nonhigh vowel even before a syllabic (reduplicative) suffix (kéli-kel, but nuté-nut), and retracted off a schwa nucleus to a preceding full vowel. For polysyllabic bases the two rules pick different syllables (Skorik jará-ŋa, reqoká-lgən, migcirét-ək vs Dunn-predicted já.ra.ŋa, ré.qo.ka.lgən, míg.ci.ret.ək). 1025.prule: Holguin 1607 (Cuzco-based Standard Colonial Quechua): accent always on the penultimate syllable of the word, never the ultima; every added particle moves it to the new penult (colla'na > collana'ca, runacu'na > runacuna'huan > runacunalla'huan); ay/au/iu/ao/ey count as one syllable for the count (ri'may, yachachi'quey, hua'yao); Spanish loans re-stressed penult (qui'cas). Santo Tomas 1560 (coastal 'lengua general'; Glottolog's MED for clas1251) describes a different system. Nouns: disyllables on the first syllable; words of three or more syllables on the penult (yaco'lla, Amao'ta, Vcuma'ri), but trisyllables whose first vowel is followed by two consonants on the first (co'ngori, to'ngori); a disyllable with an added particle, suffix or case marker keeps its accent where it was (ma'cholla, n~o'cacta), and oblique/suffixed forms of any length keep the accent of the simple form (c,ayn~a'ta > c,ayn~a'taguan, c,ayn~a'talla), except ablative -manta (own accent on ma'n), the n~ocanchic forms (accent on chic) and plural -cona, which takes the accent onto the new penult (guarmeco'na, carico'na). Verbs: 1sg indicative forms and present participles/first supines of any length on the first syllable (Mi'cuni, ri'cucuni, Ma'canacoc, Po'ricoc); otherwise a vowel standing before two consonants in the base or in a 'cremento' takes the accent (Micu'rcani, Micurca'ngui, Micuchissurcanguichi'cman), -chic plural persons keep the singular's accented syllable (Micu'nguichic), past participles and ablative gerunds penult (macanacu'spa, llu'llaspa); no verb is ever accented on the ultima; accent distinguishes Coya'scayquichic 'cosa amada de vosotros' from Coyasca'yquichic 'amaros he'.
1025.srule: No secondary or rhythmic accent in either work. Santo Tomás 1560 (cap. 25, preamble) states that the acute accent 'no es mas de vno alomenos sensible, en cada termino incõplexo' -- no more than one perceptible accent in each simple word (illustrated with Amaóta: not on a, ma or ta, only on o). González Holguín 1607 (Libro II cap. 51) gives four rules that all locate the single word accent and closes 'otra cosa notable, desta materia de acentos no lo hay'.

1026.dq: they always, or nearly always, put the tone on the penult, when the word ends in a simple vowel
1026.heavy: final syllable closed (ends in a consonant) or ending in a diphthong (e.g. -au, -ui, -eu); a final simple vowel (including long vowels, e.g. eto, nite, sobe) does not attract the tone
1026.prule: Tradition-dependent. West Syriac (Maronite) reading tradition: tone on the final syllable when it is closed or ends in a diphthong, otherwise (word ending in a simple vowel) on the penult -- 'always, or almost always'. East Syriac (Nestorian) tradition: tone on the penult throughout (quantity-insensitive). Nöldeke's historical reconstruction: originally the final syllable invariably bore the principal accent.
1026.srule: Exists, placement not given: 'Occasionally a secondary tone also becomes perceptible' (Nöldeke 1904 §56, of the present-day reading pronunciation; no position or conditions stated). For the classical, ultimate-stress stage Brockelmann 1912 §36 places a secondary accent (Nebenaccent) on the penult in many words, especially strong on long vowels.

morph.stmt: Root-and-pattern Semitic morphology with affixation on both sides but a suffixal lean in inflection: 'The different Persons, Genders, and Numbers are indicated in the Perfect by terminations, and in the Imperfect by prefixes, or by prefixes together with terminations... the Imperative... is inflected by terminations only' (Nöldeke §158B); nouns take suffixal number/state endings and possessive suffixes (§70, §65, §145), object pronouns are suffixed to the verb (§184), while derivation uses prefixes ʾeṯ- (reflexive/passive), ʾa- (causative), m- (participles, infinitive, nouns) alongside suffixes -ūṯ, -ān, -ōn, and the particles w-, b-, l-, d- are proclitic.

1027.dq: In Coahuitlán Totonac, I describe two levels of syllable prominence: lexical stress and phrase accent. Lexical stress is largely predictable for simple and complex words, and can be seen with words in isolation. Phrase accent is part of a phonological phrase (3.2): within the phrase, accent is attracted to syllables with lexical stress, but other lexical items lose prominence.

1030.prule: Lexical accent system. Every full word has exactly one primary stress. Phonological default: stress the rightmost vowel of the word (Czaykowska-Higgins 1985 'Columbian Stress Rule': grid-mark on the rightmost entry; per Zimmermann/Cz-H 1993a the rightmost UNDERLYING vowel, and if the word has no underlying vowel the initial epenthetic vowel = default-to-opposite). This default is overridden by idiosyncratic lexical stress marking on roots AND suffixes: morphemes fall into arbitrary classes with no surface or morphological-category correlate (1985: Kinkade's strong/variable/weak, recast as lexically stress-marked vs unmarked morphemes; 1993a per Zimmermann: roots S, SE, W, WE; suffixes D, D*, R, R*) that compete for the single main stress along a preference hierarchy (Zimmermann (7): D* > SE/WE ~ D > S > R* > R > W), with the rightmost winner among equally ranked morphemes ('in a sequence of two (or more) lexically stressed morphemes, the rightmost will be stressed', 1985).
1030.srule: Marginal, optional and non-rhythmic. Czaykowska-Higgins 1985 sec. 4.1: only 111 of c. 3,500 words are marked for secondary stress, with no consistent pattern; where marked it precedes the primary - on the root (primary on the rightmost suffix with an underlying vowel), on the first of two stressed suffixes, or in compounds on the left root or the joiner -a-/-aɬ- (primary on the rightmost root or suffix); Kinkade's pretonic open-syllable secondary stress with lengthening she takes to be length, not stress. Czaykowska-Higgins 1989 fn. 11 doubts secondary stress is rule-assigned at all (c. 2% of forms; likely unreduced unstressed vowels). Zimmermann 2018 sec. 3.3 (on Cz-H 1993a data): undeleted unstressed suffix vowels before the main stress carry an optional secondary stress (niʔk'əmàn'kákst), at most one per word.

1031.prule: Word stress is lexically specified within a right-edge three-syllable window: words are oxytone (final), paroxytone (penultimate) or proparoxytone (antepenultimate); position is not predictable from segmental shape or weight in any reached source and is not marked in the orthography except (coincidentally) on oxytones, whose final grave accent (aletta) primarily signals a following strong (non-lenited) consonant. evidence_works.detail: Cupeño primary stress is lexical: an accented root keeps its stress over any accented affix, a word with an unaccented root stresses the rightmost accented affix, and a word with no accented morpheme takes default initial stress; within roots long vowels attract stress and otherwise initial vs. peninitial stress is contrastive, with one stress peak per word and no secondary stress. morph.elicq: Ebina 2011 gives no statement of how stress was determined; the whole accent section is: 'Cusco Quechua is a stress-accent language. Stress falls on the penultimate syllable and is non-distinctive.' (§2.3, p.6). The volume preface says only that each sketch is based on 'the primary data researched by' the author; the impressionistic remark in §4.6 ('The second nominal has a clear stress on the penultimate syllable. The stress of the first nominal is not very clear') suggests auditory judgement but names no elicitation setting. 1035.tone: Source treats stress, length and tempo as concomitants of the word-level tonal nucleus: H nucleus = extra intensity + fast tempo, L nucleus = extra length + slow tempo; 'The contrastive intensity of the nuclear syllable seems to be of more importance than the correct tone on that syllable' (p.150). Nucleus tone (H vs L) is contrastive in 1-3 syllable words and nucleus position in 2-3 syllable words (minimal pairs for 1-2 syllable words; 'Minimal pairs in words beyond two syllables have not been found', p.152, so trisyllabic contrasts are shown with non-minimal pairs); in trisyllables a final-syllable nucleus tone 'seems to vary'. Orthography note (p.158): 'Because of much fluctuation in tone... tone only needs to be marked on minimal sets.' A reviewer could alternatively read this as lexical accent (free nucleus position with intensity), i.e. a pitch-accent system; either way there is no fixed or weight-based stress rule.

tn.quote: Like most other North Germanic varieties in Sweden and Norway, Elfdalian distinguishes two pitch accents, traditionally called acute accent and grave accent, or accent 1 and accent 2, marked here using the non-IPA diacritics acute and grave accent. The pitch accent is phonemic: changing the accent of a word can change the meaning in a few cases ... Phonetically in focus position, the acute accent is realised as a rising-falling tone ... The grave accent is realised as a falling tone in the stressed syllable that rises again in the post-tonic syllable, giving it a ‘double-peak accent’

evidence_works.detail: Measured: vowel and consonant durations (waveforms with spectrograms) and F0 peak alignment (H-quotient, tone curves over spectrograms, Praat) in read frame sentences recorded 1990/1991 and 2008 from informants in Sollerön, Östre Mora (Nusnäs, Garsås) and Skattungbyn, i.e. varieties of dale1238 other than Elfdalian: 'Analysen er utført ved hjelp av analyseprogrammet Praat. Durasjonsmålene er først og fremst basert på målinger i bølgeformer (waveforms) med støtte av korresponderende spektrogrammer. Måling av tonegang er gjort i tonekurver lagt over spektrogrammer' (p. 12); 'Den bygger på forfatterens eget feltarbeid' (p. 1). For Elfdalian itself the work restates earlier work rather than measuring: 'Nyström (1991) og Kristoffersen (1990; 1991; 2007b; 2008) viser imidlertid at både når det gjelder Älvdalsmålet og Nord-Gudbrandsdalsmålet er tonegangen i jamvektsord klart en forkortet utgave av tonelag 2-melodien, slik at jamvektsaksent og vanlig tonelag 2 kan ses på som komplementært fordelte varianter av samme strukturelle enhet, nemlig tonelag 2' (p. 8), so the 'level-stress' (jamvekt) words of Elfdalian are accent-2 words with a short root syllable and root-initial stress stands. Finding for a sister variety inside the languoid: 'Vi har sett at i Östre Mora, representert ved Nusnäs og Garsås, er rotstavelsen i gamle jamvektsord bevart kort, mens endestavelsen er blitt forlenget og har fått trykket' (§5.3, p. 36), i.e. final stress in the old short-root disyllable class in Östre Mora (Moramål), a within-languoid difference from the Elfdalian coding.

evidence_works.detail: Impressionistic dialectological description. Levander explicitly sets stress placement aside and treats the accents: 'Utan att närmare ingå varken på frågan om den musikaliska accenten, vilken är ytterligt svårutredd, eller på frågan om olika stavelsers tryckstyrka i förhållande till varandra ("betoning", intensitet), vilken bäst behandlas i samband med det följande, övergår jag direkt till att behandla de olika s. k. taktformerna i dalmålet' (pp. 49-50). He describes a third accent in short-root polysyllables with stress and pitch evenly distributed in Elfdalian: 'Dalmålet har dessa två accenter men dessutom också en tredje, som enklast kan kallas jämviktsaccent, och som uppträder i två- eller flerstaviga, kortstaviga ord. I forndalskan — liksom ännu i Älvdalsmålet — torde den ha utmärkts av att både tryckstyrka och tonhöjd voro påfallande jämnt fördelade på stavelserna, så att man mången gång kan vara tveksam om, på vilken stavelse huvudtonen ligger' (p. 50). Also p. 50: monosyllables can carry grave accent ('enstaviga ord kunna ha grav accent'), a deviation from Standard Swedish accentuation.

1040.prule: Word accent stays on the same syllable as in (Vulgar) Latin, i.e. inherited lexical position; words are oxytone, paroxytone or proparoxytone (Bartoli marks accent on all proparoxytones, all oxytones and consonant-final paroxytones, leaving vowel-final paroxytones unmarked as the commonest type). No synchronic positional or weight rule is stated; Latin quantity is lost ('Geschichte der Quantität... dunkel').
1040.srule: Not mentioned in Bartoli 1906 vol. II, 'Akzent und Quantität' §§ 267-269 and 280-282 (printed 316-318, 327-328): one inherited word accent per word is described, and 'Vom Silben- und Satzakzente kann man hier nichts Bestimmtes sagen'; the Hauptton/Nebenton labels of §§ 311-325 classify Latin unstressed-vowel positions, not Vegliote secondary stress. Later works (Hadlich 1965/1998, Swiggers 1998, Maiden 2020) are also silent.

secx.sec_quote_tr: Of syllable and sentence accent nothing definite can be said here ... [§ 311] Pretonic vowels: cantárono [scan 'cantdrond'] (where a is pre-main-tonic and o pre-secondary-tonic). This grouping cannot be justified in detail here; it suffices to refer to the two introductory §§ 312 and 319.

dfl.pattern: Majority pattern per Maiden 2020: word stress is 'usually oxytonic or paroxytonic' (final or penultimate), proparoxytones being marginal and mostly loanwords...
dfl.note: Majority pattern per Maiden 2020: word stress is 'usually oxytonic or paroxytonic' (final or penultimate), proparoxytones being marginal and mostly loanwords; no single default syllable is named and no rule predicts final vs penult (lexical, inherited from Latin/Romance, many oxytones from apocope). Bartoli is consistent: his transcription convention (§ 269, vol. II col. 318) marks the accent on all proparoxytones, all oxytones and consonant-final paroxytones and leaves vowel-final paroxytones…
dfl.q: Word-stress is usually oxytonic or paroxytonic, many oxytones having arisen, historically, through the extensive deletion of word-final unstressed vowels; the proparoxytones tend to be loanwords from Italo-Romance or Slavonic.

evidence_works.detail: Encyclopedia synthesis of Udaina's Vegliote as recorded by Bartoli (the same subsection cites Bartoli 1906/2000:II§263 and II§276; the summary says Vegliote 'is principally represented by the linguistic testimony of its last speaker, Tuone Udaina', explored 'principally by Matteo Bartoli'). No first-hand observation is possible (extinct); no measurement. It states: 'Word-stress is usually oxytonic or paroxytonic, many oxytones having arisen, historically, through the extensive deletion of word-final unstressed vowels; the proparoxytones tend to be loanwords from Italo-Romance or Slavonic.' (p. 2) and 'We have no information about intonation or syllable structure... Nor is there any evidence for synchronic length distinctions.' (p. 2). Adds an explicit synchronic placement summary (final or penultimate, antepenultimate marginal and mostly borrowed) that the entry's Bartoli quotes only imply.
